C0.quote: We study individual manipulability of social choice rules under incomplete information

C1.quote: we study when non-manipulability is inherited from one model to another
C1.note: Computed manipulability indexes (exact enumeration, coded as SI) plus theoretical propositions on non-manipulability; all about manipulation incentives.

C2.1.quote: A preference profile of all voters is denoted by

C2.2.quote: it is assumed to be a linear order
C2.2.note: Voters report linear orders; PIF outputs are polls.

C2.3.quote: all voters report their sincere preferences to an opinion poll
C2.3.note: Preferences are held; manipulation means misrepresenting them.

C2.4.quote: voters can achieve a better voting result by misrepresenting their preferences
C2.4.note: Sincere preferences vs strategic reports are distinguished (P̃i vs Pi).

C3.1.quote: a voter has an incentive to manipulate under a given PIF
C3.1.note: All analyses concern manipulation incentives of voters.

C4.1.note: Voter preferences are strict orders over alternatives and no utility/welfare notions are used for voters; the only 'better off' is defined via Pi.

C5.1.note: Outcomes are evaluated by manipulability indexes, not welfare, efficiency or representation.

VOT.quote_behav: A voter having an incentive to manipulate individually with some strategy
VOT.quote_info: shows what kind of information is known by a voter about P
VOT.note: Voters are potential manipulators, with information given by the PIF (ranges from complete Profile-PIF to 1Winner). Other voters are sincere in Model 1.

C8.1.note: The incentive to manipulate is an existence-of-strategy condition (weak dominance over sincere voting under uncertainty). Models 2 and 3 are level-2 / cognitive-hierarchy style bounded rationality.

C9.1.note: Claims about real-world manipulability and the immunity of rules.

C9.2.quote: it does not make much sense
C9.2.note: The claim that manipulation makes little sense requires that voters demand a strategy that never makes them worse off (stated as 'seems quite natural'); that voters actually know only poll information or hold the assumed beliefs about others is not argued empirically; the 'immunity in reality' claim also needs a link between incentive and actual manipulation, which is acknowledged as unmeasured.
